newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian refiners struggle to meet EU gas oil rule.
newsitem.headline: Russian refiners struggle to meet EU gas oil rule.

text.p: Few Russian oil refiners are ready to meet a new European rule requiring "greener" gas oil by October, which could force the search for new markets, analysts said on Tuesday.
Only five of Russia's 28 refineries can make the greener material.
An EC directive requires all automotive gas oil, or diesel, to have a sulphur content no higher than 0.05 percent by October 1, well below the current maximum 0.2 percent.
Russia traditionally supplies much of Europe with high-sulphur gas oil, used as diesel (automotive) fuel and as heating fuel, especially in Germany.

"Russian oil products are going to go further afield," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of oil and gas at MC Securities in London. "We'll see products looking for markets where restrictions are less tight, because the margins for selling into Europe will go down."
But one senior Russian trader said even those refineries ready to meet the directive -- Norsi, Kirishi, Omsk, Ufa and Perm -- faced challenges.
"I don't think we'll see any immediate changes in Russia's total export volumes of gas oil, because the fundamentals in Europe have to change first," he said.
Russia produced about 47 million tonnes of diesel last year, of which it exported about 20 million tonnes.
Russian and Baltic oil products export pipelines are unable to batch product from individual Russian refineries, leaving green diesel mixed with dirtier material from other plants.

The Latvian port of Ventspils, Russia's leading diesel export outlet, has problems with bacteria that contaminate and spoil quality. Two other Baltic outlets, Riga and Tallinn, do not have quality control problems, but they can handle only smaller vessels of 10,000 tonnes or so.
The five Russian refineries also face problems in disposing of heavy sulphuric acids generated during processing, which could initially inhibit them from cranking up output.
One Russian trader said strong premiums would encourage the other, non-green refineries to invest in or retool hydrotreating and desulphurisation units to lower sulphur levels.

"People will build desulphurisation capacity and hunt for markets -- African, South American, Carribean, the Far East, but they'll wake up that it's better to sell to Europe," O'Sullivan said. "There will be step-by-step changes (in export patterns)."

While energy analyst James Bunch of Renaissance Capital said Russia could find it tough to find markets for excess diesel, he said some material could head to North America for processing into lighter products.
Traders said they did not know what capacities were at Russia's five "green" refineries, saying only that they were operating at about half of their total potential capacity.
